name: Pit hair laser removal

lead: Laser removal gives smooth underarms for months without shaving, and some people hope the missing hair also means less odor.

Light is absorbed by dark hair pigment and damages the follicle. A 2006 meta-analysis described on Wikipedia found alexandrite and diode lasers reduced hair by about 50 percent for up to six months. Laser hair removal has been FDA-approved in the US since 1997. The studies reviewed measured hair reduction, not odor.

paras: Done in a clinic over a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, on shaved skin. Hair thins gradually across the series.
Side effects are reported as temporary, and were more frequent with diode lasers than alexandrite or intense pulsed light in one 2006 comparison. Darker skin tones need device and clinic care.

angle.text: Laser hair removal gives lasting smooth underarms, and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to reduce armpit odor by removing hair. Studies show about 50 percent hair reduction for up to six months; they did not test odor.

lead: Underarm laser hair removal uses pulses of light absorbed by dark hair pigment to damage hair follicles so that armpit hair grows back thinner, finer or not at all. It relies on selective photothermolysis, matching wavelength and pulse length so the hair and follicle absorb the energy while nearby skin is largely spared.[1] Laser hair removal reached the market in 1995 to 1996 and was approved by the US FDA in 1997.[2][1]

For appearance, the appeal is a smooth, stubble-free underarm without daily shaving, fewer ingrown hairs and razor bumps, and for some people a cleaner-smelling armpit. In looksmaxxing circles the procedure is also discussed as a lasting way to reduce armpit odor by removing the hair; users on T Nation have long described shaving the pits and laser-treating other body areas as part of grooming.[3]

A 2006 meta-analysis described on Wikipedia found alexandrite and diode lasers reduced hair by about 50 percent for up to six months, with no evidence of benefit from intense pulsed light, Nd:YAG or ruby lasers.[2] No published study has tested laser hair removal specifically for body odor.

paras: The laser targets pigment in the hair so that follicles are destroyed. Wikipedia's hair removal article says permanence sometimes follows several sessions and that the number needed depends on the amount and type of hair.[2] Melanin is the target: eumelanin in brown and black hair absorbs light well, while pheomelanin in blonde and red hair does not, which is why light hair responds poorly.[1] Cooling methods such as contact cooling, cryogen spray and cold air protect the epidermis and allow higher energy levels.[1]

Ruby (694 nm) lasers are used for pale skin, alexandrite (755 nm) for all skin types, pulsed diode (810 nm) for pale to medium skin and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) for dark skin; intense pulsed light is a filtered flash rather than a laser.[1] Light skin with dark hair gives the best results, while light, red, gray and white hair and fine vellus hair generally respond poorly.[1]

Most people need at least about eight treatments, three to eight weeks apart depending on the area, and treated hairs shed over two to three weeks; Wikipedia says pulling them out is discouraged because of infection risk.[1] Under the FDA's definition, permanent hair reduction means a long-term stable decrease in regrowth rather than total removal, and many patients see some regrowth in later years.[1]

Proponents argue that without hair, bacteria and sweat have less to cling to and odor is reduced for longer than with shaving. Wikipedia's hair removal article says hair can collect odor-causing microorganisms.[2] The body odor article says odor arises from skin bacteria acting on apocrine sweat, and it notes that armpit hair helps spread odors; it does not discuss hair removal.[4]

The underarm hair article says the purpose of the hair is unclear: proposed roles include wicking sweat and odor-causing bacteria away from the skin, reducing friction, and trapping odor and strengthening pheromones, though some of these claims are weakly sourced.[5] A 2012 study cited there reported that shaved armpits were rated as no different in odor pleasantness from unshaved ones.[5]

Wikipedia reports that in one randomized trial diode laser reduced hair by 69.2 percent at 12 months compared with 52.7 percent for intense pulsed light, and that a small 2000 study found laser faster and less painful than electrolysis, which can remove hair completely but is slower.[1] The 2006 meta-analysis found about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers.[2]

A 2006 comparison reported more side effects with diode lasers than with alexandrite lasers or intense pulsed light, and described them as temporary.[2] Itching, pinkness, redness and swelling usually resolve within a few days; acne flare-ups and skin discoloration are the most common serious effects, usually when energy reaches surrounding skin, and other risks include burns, hypopigmentation, scabbing, purpura and infection.[1] Numbing creams carry danger when applied over large areas.[1]
Regulation varies: in the US the FDA oversees devices while most states regulate for-hire services, and some limit use to physicians or supervised staff.[1]

Underarm hair removal by shaving or other means is common in some cultures, particularly among women.[5] Wikipedia notes that the technique was tested experimentally for about twenty years before reaching the market, with research by R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman on selectively targeting follicles leading to clinical use in 1996.[1] Consumer at-home devices are widely available.[1]

On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, users have described trimming or shaving body hair and getting areas such as the back lasered as part of preparing a physique, with underarm shaving mentioned as routine.[3]

No studies found on laser hair removal for body odor. General efficacy findings for laser hair removal on hair reduction are described above: a 2006 meta-analysis (alexandrite and diode about 50 percent reduction for up to six months) and a randomized trial of diode laser versus intense pulsed light (69.2 percent versus 52.7 percent at 12 months).[2][1] A clinical trial registered as NCT06140199 involves laser in pilonidal disease, a different condition.[6]

lore.intro: Underarm laser removal is discussed in grooming and bodybuilding forums mainly as a smooth-skin and odor-reduction measure.[3]

claims.claim: Removing pit hair permanently reduces body odor.
Laser can make underarm hair removal permanent.
Hair removal is only worthwhile on dark hair.
